title: Homing pigeons can find their loft from unfamiliar places.
hook: A map made of smells, a clock that reads the sun, and a magnetic sense inside the body.

levels.title: The pigeon is the address, not the postman.

objects.title: It can only deliver to its own home
objects.text: A messenger pigeon is raised to recognise a home loft, then carried somewhere else and released with a tiny message. It flies back to that loft. To send messages both ways, you need birds with homes at both ends; a pigeon cannot simply be told a new address.

levels.title: Finding home requires both a map and a compass.

objects.title: Four clues do different jobs

image.alt: Conceptual diagram of smell, sun, magnetic and landmark cues during a homing journey.
image.credit: Locally supplied conceptual illustration; not a measured route or universal navigation algorithm.

objects.caption: Smell can help locate a region, sun and magnetic cues provide direction, and familiar landmarks help near home. This schematic simplifies overlapping strategies.

objects.title: Four clues do four different jobs
objects.text: Smell patterns may tell a pigeon which region it has been dropped in: a map. The sun's position plus the bird's internal clock can give a bearing: a compass. Earth's magnetic field can supply another directional cue. Recognised roads, rivers and buildings help refine the approach near home.

objects.title: It does not calculate GPS coordinates
objects.text: Researchers infer overlapping navigational strategies from experiments that alter individual clues. They have not found a single universal algorithm inside the pigeon. Some cues are most useful far from home; familiar landmarks become more valuable as the loft gets close.

levels.title: The air above a landscape carries a chemical map.

objects.title: A smell can hint at which side of home you are on
objects.text: At its loft, a young pigeon experiences different odour mixtures arriving on winds from different directions. The olfactory-map hypothesis says it learns those associations. At an unfamiliar release site, the local mixture can help it estimate displacement from home—not by simply following one smell plume like a dog.

sources.title: Homing Pigeons Only Navigate in Air with Intact Environmental Odours

objects.title: Filtering the air spoiled their first hour
objects.text: In a 2011 GPS study, birds taken 53 or 61 km away in ordinary air oriented better than birds transported in charcoal-filtered air. Puffs of arbitrary floral smells did not restore their orientation. Natural environmental odours appeared to carry geographical information, not merely switch on a different sense.

sources.title: Homing Pigeons Only Navigate in Air with Intact Environmental Odours

objects.title: Scientists measured real gradients in the air
objects.description: Researchers measured regional gradients of airborne compounds, including sea-derived dimethyl sulfide and plant-related chemicals, around a Tuscan loft. The gradients could form a smell map; the paper does not prove exactly which molecules individual pigeons read.

levels.title: The sun moves. The pigeon corrects for the time.

objects.title: Try the pigeon navigation lab
objects.description: Change smell, sun, magnetic and landmark clues to watch an illustrative route respond. This simplified model is not a prediction of a real flight.

objects.title: The same sun position means different things at different hours
objects.text: Because the sun crosses the sky through the day, its location alone does not label north or south. A pigeon combines its apparent position with an internal daily clock to infer a compass bearing. The bird is accounting for the sun's motion rather than expecting it to stay still.

sources.title: Orientation by pigeons: is the sun necessary?

objects.title: To shift the sun, scientists actually shift the bird's clock
objects.text: Researchers change a pigeon's light-dark schedule so it thinks, for example, that it is several hours later. Under a visible sun, the bird's initial heading shifts in the predicted direction. When clouds hide the sun, other cues can partly take over. The real sun never moved in the experiment.

levels.title: The magnetic sense may involve both ear and liver.

objects.title: A 2026 brain study found a light-independent signal
objects.text: Magnetic stimulation activated circuits connected with the pigeon inner ear. Researchers also found specialised cells compatible with sensing tiny electrical effects from motion through a magnetic field. That supports an electromagnetic-induction model, but a complete signal-to-navigation pathway has not yet been demonstrated.

sources.title: A global screen for magnetically induced neuronal activity in the pigeon brain

objects.title: Removing certain immune cells disrupted cloudy-day orientation
objects.text: Another 2026 study identified iron-bearing macrophages in pigeon livers. When researchers depleted these cells, birds lost much of their usual orientation under overcast skies, but not with visible sun. The authors propose a magnetic sensory role; how the signal reaches the brain remains uncertain.

sources.title: Homing pigeon navigation relies on superparamagnetic macrophages under overcast conditions

objects.title: An earlier magnetic-beak discovery was overturned
objects.description: Structures once described as magnetosensitive nerve cells in pigeon beaks were identified as iron-rich immune cells instead. It is a warning: finding a magnetic material in an animal does not prove that it is a working compass.

levels.title: Near home, pigeons sometimes follow highways.

objects.title: They sometimes choose a longer, familiar route
objects.text: Researchers analysed 216 GPS-recorded flights around Rome. Experienced pigeons were attracted to highways, rail lines and particular junctions, even when those routes were less direct than a straight flight home. Road-following was significant on roughly 40–50% of tracks from certain release directions, not every flight.

sources.title: Pigeon homing along highways and exits

objects.title: Some highway exits became turning points
objects.description: The GPS traces show that pigeons repeatedly crossed selected topographical points, particularly near their loft. Following landmarks can be a reliable learned strategy even when it increases distance travelled.

levels.title: Some birds navigate an ocean on their first migration.

objects.title: A young godwit crossed the Pacific without stopping
objects.text: In October 2022, a juvenile bar-tailed godwit nicknamed B6 made an approximately 13,560 km non-stop flight from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days. Its solar-powered satellite transmitter tracked a first migration over open sea, far beyond the familiar landmarks available to a homing pigeon near its loft.

sources.title: Juvenile Bar-tailed Godwit B6 Sets World Record

objects.title: The transmitter revealed the full journey
objects.publisher: University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, 2022
objects.description: Scientists fitted the young bird with a miniature tracker before it departed. The 11-day record reveals what it accomplished, not which precise sensory algorithm guided it over the Pacific. That part of animal navigation remains an open scientific question.
